title: Ananda's grief
hookLine: Ananda's verses after the passing: the friend is gone, all directions are dark (Theragatha, Ananda)
last: AS A SERVANT WAITS FOR WAGES.

cards: All the directions go dark. A friend is gone, the teacher is gone, and the ground goes out from under him. That moment is in the verses of Ananda, the Buddha's attendant.
Tradition says he walked beside the teacher for years, looked after his needs, and remembered what he taught.
After a run of calm voices, men who have put the burden down, today sits with that moment, and with what he found to hold on to.

teach.b: First, the line. All the directions are dark, he says. The teachings aren't clear to me.
The good friend has gone, and everything seems dark. Second, whose death. The verses speak of a friend gone and of a teacher passed away.
Tradition links these lines to the death of Sariputta, whose calm came yesterday, and to the passing of the Buddha.

In one sutta, when word of Sariputta's death reaches Ananda, he tells the Buddha that his body feels unsteady, the directions aren't clear to him, and the teachings won't come to mind. Third, what's surprising.

This sits in a book of freed men, and here is a long-time follower saying grief has knocked the teaching right out of his head. The collection keeps his words as they are. Fourth, what he does with it.

teach.h: A FRIEND GONE, A TEACHER GONE.
teach.b: In the same verses, Ananda says that for one whose friend has gone and whose teacher has passed, there's no friend like mindfulness of the body.
When the people are gone, what's left to hold is this breath, this body, here.

teach.h: NO FRIEND LIKE THE BODY'S MINDFULNESS.
teach.b: And in the sutta, the Buddha answers him with what he had always taught: everything dear and pleasing will change and be parted from us. How could it be otherwise?
He doesn't scold the grief. He reminds Ananda where to stand inside it. In these verses, grief isn't kept out of the practice.
It's where the practice goes next.

how: Buddhist teachers often turn to Ananda's grief, and the Buddha's reply about the parting from all that is dear, when they speak with people who are mourning, and some point to his verse on mindfulness of the body as a friend that stays.

o: Ananda's sorrow when his friend and teacher died
Ananda's fear of living alone in the forest
Ananda's homesickness for his family's town

s: the Theragatha leaves out the elders' grief
Ananda's verses keep it: all the directions are dark, the teachings aren't clear.
Ananda says there's no friend like mindfulness of the body
for one whose friend and teacher are gone, he says, that is the friend that's left.
in the sutta, the Buddha scolds Ananda for grieving
he reminds him that everything dear will change and be parted from us.

games.q: you're Ananda. word comes that Sariputta has died, and everything goes dark. what do you do?
o: say nothing. a monk shouldn't grieve.
go to the Buddha and tell him how it is.
games.why: in the sutta he tells the Buddha his body feels unsteady and the directions aren't clear to him. the Buddha answers with the teaching on parting from all that is dear.

practice: Let one face come, a friend who's gone, whether they died, moved away or simply drifted, and notice where you feel it, the chest, the throat, behind the eyes, without pushing it off or digging for more.

Then, like Ananda, rest some attention in the body itself, the weight in the chair, the breath going in and out: the friend in the mind, the breath in the body. If it gets too heavy, open your eyes and look around the room.

wordCard.voice: Ananda's grief. The attendant's verses when friend and teacher had gone: all directions dark, and mindfulness of the body as the friend that stays. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: disa, a direction. Ananda says all the directions are dark to him.

carryVoice: Your line: all directions dark. Even grief has a place to stand. Go gently; see you tomorrow.
